stages.name: Measuring GDP
stages.title: Measuring GDP
stages.sub: How economists measure the size of an economy and its growth, without being fooled by prices, population or inflation.

steps.q: Farms, factories and shops sell goods and services this year. What would the total value of everything sold tell you?
steps.right: The size of the whole economy's output
steps.wrong: Only the profit made by firms
steps.hint: Think about adding up every good and service sold in the whole country, not just one firm's profit.

steps.q: Prices rise 10% but the country makes exactly as much as last year. Does GDP in today's prices show output has grown?
steps.right: No, it just looks bigger from prices
steps.hint: If nothing extra was made but prices went up, has more actually been produced?

steps.q: Country A has a bigger GDP than B, but three times as many people. Does that mean each person is better off?
steps.right: Not necessarily, it depends on population
steps.wrong: Yes, a bigger GDP always means better off
steps.hint: If the same GDP is shared between far more people, what happens to the amount each person gets?

steps.q: A country sells as many cars as last year, each at a higher price. Has the amount made changed?
steps.right: No, the amount made is unchanged
steps.hint: Count the cars, not the price tag on them. Has the number of cars changed?

steps.wrong: The raw money totals each year
